clause.text: Any person detained shall be brought before a judge and cannot be held without legal order.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the petitioner was unlawfully detained without being produced before a Magistrate or without a valid detention order, violating Article 13(2) of the Constitution.
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioner claimed he was arrested on 23.07.91 and detained unlawfully at Eheliyagoda Police Station until 06.08.91 without a valid detention order and without being produced before a Magistrate, thus violating his fundamental rights under Article 13(2).
case_context.respondent_argument: The respondents argued the petitioner was arrested on 06.08.91, and detention was authorized under Emergency Regulations, implying lawful detention.
key_facts: Petitioner was arrested on 23.07.91 (not 06.08.91 as claimed by respondents).
Petitioner detained at Eheliyagoda Police Station from 23.07.91 to 06.08.91 without valid detention order or being produced before a Magistrate.
Detention order under Regulation 19(2) authorized detention at Pelawatte Detention Camp, but petitioner was held at Deraniyagala Police Station.
No material was presented to show further investigations justifying detention under Regulation 19(2).
Preventive detention order under Regulation 17(1) dated 02.11.91 regularized detention at Deraniyagala Police Station.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The Court held that Article 13(2) requires that any detained person must be brought before a judge and cannot be held without a legal order. Detention without a valid order or judicial oversight is unlawful. Detention under Regulation 19(2) must be for further investigations and authorized properly. The petitioner’s detention from 23.07.91 to 06.08.91 without a valid order and not being produced before a Magistrate was unlawful.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The Court found the petitioner was indeed arrested on 23.07.91 and detained unlawfully at Eheliyagoda Police Station until 06.08.91 without a valid detention order or judicial production. The detention order under Regulation 19(2) was invalid as it authorized detention at a different location and lacked evidence of further investigations. The preventive detention order dated 02.11.91 was lawful and regularized subsequent detention.
principles_established: Detention without a valid legal order and without being brought before a judge violates Article 13(2).
Detention orders must specify lawful place of detention and be supported by material justifying detention.
Detention under emergency regulations must be for further investigations to be lawful.
precedents_cited: Nanayakkara v. Henry Perera [1985] 2 Sri LR 375
Chandra Kalyani Perera v. Captain Siriwardena [1992] 1 Sri LR 251
Wimal Vidyamuni v. Col. Jayatilleke S.C. Application No. 852/91
Ratnapala v. Hector Dharmasiri S.C. Application No. 162/91

outcome.holding: The Court held that the petitioner’s detention from 23.07.91 to 06.08.91 was unlawful under Article 13(2) as he was not produced before a judge and no valid detention order authorized that detention. The preventive detention order dated 02.11.91 was lawful. The petitioner’s fundamental rights under Article 13(2) were infringed.
outcome.remedy_or_orders: The Court granted a declaration of infringement of fundamental rights and awarded compensation totaling Rs. 40,000 to the petitioner, with costs.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 13(2) is central to the Court’s reasoning as it protects against unlawful detention without judicial oversight or valid legal authority. The Court’s finding of unlawful detention directly relied on this constitutional guarantee.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The Court found the petitioner was detained from 23.07.91 to 06.08.91 without a valid detention order and without being produced before a Magistrate, which was unlawful under Article 13(2). The detention order under Regulation 19(2) authorized detention at Pelawatte but the petitioner was held at Deraniyagala Police Station.
